nameStory: The white bog orchid gets its name from its pristine white flowers and its love of boggy, wet places. It's also called 'bog candle' because its tall spike of white flowers can look like a glowing candle rising from the dark, wet ground of marshes and swamps.
description: The white bog orchid is a striking native wildflower that produces a tall spike of small, pure white flowers rising 1-3 feet above wet ground. Each flower spike is densely packed with dozens of tiny orchid blooms, creating an impressive white column. The plant has several narrow, lance-shaped leaves that clasp around the base of the stem, and like all orchids, each flower has a distinctive lip and spur.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense spike of small, pure white orchid flowers with a sweet, intensely spicy fragrance reminiscent of cloves - you can often smell it before you see it

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single tall stem rising 1-3 feet from wet ground, topped with a cylindrical flower spike that can be 2-8 inches long

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Several narrow, lance-shaped leaves that wrap around the stem base, getting smaller as they go up the stem

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Each tiny flower has a distinctive orchid shape with a protruding spur at the back and a white lip that may have a slight greenish tinge

habitat: Look for white bog orchid in cold, wet places like cedar swamps, tamarack bogs, calcareous fens, and marshy meadows throughout New England. It prefers sunny or partially sunny spots in these wetlands and is often found where the soil stays consistently moist and has high mineral content.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from wet soil, with narrow leaves unfurling around the developing flower stem.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August, when the fragrant white flower spikes are most noticeable and aromatic.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed pods develop, while leaves begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground trace in the frozen wetlands.

funFact: This orchid is sometimes called 'scentbottle' because its perfume is so powerful that a single plant can fill an entire bog with its sweet, clove-like fragrance - some people can smell it from 20 feet away on a calm day!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other white bog orchids in the same genus, but the white bog orchid's intensely spicy-sweet fragrance is usually the dead giveaway - if you can smell cloves in a wetland, you've found your plant!
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'dilatata' means 'widened' or 'dilated,' referring to the expanded lip of each small flower. Despite being called a 'bog' orchid, it's equally at home in fens and swamps - any consistently wet, mineral-rich habitat will do.
compareHints: White bog orchid stands out from its Platanthera relatives by its pure white color and incredibly strong clove-like fragrance. The white-fringed orchid has more elaborate, fringed petals, while the green bog orchids lack the bright white color and distinctive spicy scent that make this species so memorable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its bog orchid relatives, this is by far the smallest and most inconspicuous - while cousins like the fringed orchids have showy white or purple flowers, the small green wood orchid is all about stealth.

Among its Platanthera relatives, the White-fringed Orchid is distinguished by its pure white color and deeply fringed petals - the Lesser and Greater Purple Fringed Orchids have similar fringed flowers but are purple, while other white bog orchids lack the dramatic fringe.
Among New England's bog orchids (Platanthera), the Lesser Purple Fringed Orchid is distinguished by its bright purple color and deeply fringed flower lips.
Among its Platanthera relatives, the ragged fringed orchid stands out for its greenish-white color and extremely irregular, deeply cut fringes.
Among its Platanthera relatives, the Greater Purple Fringed Orchid stands out for its size and deeply fringed purple petals.
Among New England's bog orchids, this species is distinguished by its greenish-white flowers and self-fertilizing habit.
Among its bog orchid relatives, green bog orchid is distinguished by its consistently greenish flowers and preference for the wettest habitats.
Among its bog orchid relatives, the Round-leaved Bog Orchid is unique for having just two large, circular basal leaves.
Among New England's bog orchids, pale green orchid stands out for its particularly subtle coloring and preference for disturbed shoreline habitats.

Among New England's bog orchids, Hooker's is distinctive for having exactly two large basal leaves lying flat on the ground, while most other Platanthera species have multiple leaves arranged up the stem.
Among its bog orchid relatives, Large-leaved Bog Orchid is unmistakable due to its two massive basal leaves - most other Platanthera species have smaller, more numerous leaves arranged up the stem.
Among its bog orchid relatives, the orange-fringed orchid is the only one with orange flowers and deeply fringed petals.
Among New England's bog orchids, this is the only one with such intensely bright orange flowers in a dense, compact cluster.

Unlike its relatives the round-leaved bog orchid (which has two large round leaves) or Hooker's orchid (which has two broad leaves that hug the ground), the blunt-leaved rein orchid typically has just one distinctively paddle-shaped leaf with a rounded tip.
Among its Platanthera relatives, Shriver's frilly orchid is distinguished by its particular fringe pattern and purple coloration.
